pos: n. (the chief of a party or faction; a leader of a movement)
etymology: Greek protostates, from protos, first, and histemi, to stand — a military term for the man standing first in the front rank. The English ringleader carries a note of ringleading a mob; the Greek is simply the man in front.
biblical_def: For we have found this man a pestilent fellow, and a mover of sedition among all the Jews throughout the world, and a ringleader of the sect of the Nazarenes. This is Tertullus the orator prosecuting Paul before Felix, and the indictment is a model of how the church has been accused ever since. Three charges are laid. Paul is a plague of a man; he stirs up sedition; and he stands at the head of a sect. The Greek behind ringleader is protostates, the soldier in the front rank — Tertullus is saying Paul leads from the front, which happens to be true. Two of the three charges are false and the accusers know it; sedition was the charge that would interest a Roman governor, which is precisely why it was made. Paul's answer does not deny the association but corrects the category: this I confess unto thee, that after the way which they call heresy, so worship I the God of my fathers, believing all things which are written in the law and in the prophets. He concedes the party label his enemies use, denies that it is a departure, and grounds his defence in the Scriptures he and his accusers share. The name Nazarenes was itself a sneer, taken from a town of which it had been asked whether any good thing could come out of it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): the leader of any association of men; a leader of a body of men engaged in the violation of law.
webster_full: RINGLEADER, n. The leader of any association of men engaged in violation of law or an illegal enterprise.
RINGLEADER, n. The leader of any association or body of men; used chiefly in an ill sense.
SEDITION, n. A factious commotion of the people, or a tumultuous assembly of men rising in opposition to law or the administration.
SECT, n. A body or number of persons united in tenets, chiefly in philosophy or religion, but constituting a distinct party.
PESTILENT, a. Producing the plague, or other malignant disease; mischievous; destructive.
scriptures: Acts 24:5
For we have found this man a pestilent fellow, and a mover of sedition among all the Jews throughout the world, and a ringleader of the sect of the Nazarenes:
Acts 24:14
But this I confess unto thee, that after the way which they call heresy, so worship I the God of my fathers, believing all things which are written in the law and in the prophets:
2 Timothy 3:5
Having a form of godliness, but denying the power thereof: from such turn away.
Hebrews 10:31
It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God.
corruption_summary: Faithfulness is still prosecuted as divisiveness, and the charge of sedition still carries where doctrinal charges would not; Paul's answer is to confess the association and correct the category.
corruption_paragraphs: Tertullus knew his tribunal. A Roman governor did not care what Paul believed about the resurrection, so the indictment was translated into terms Rome would act on: disorder, faction, a movement with a leader at the front of it. The pattern is permanent. Where a doctrinal objection would gain no traction, the charge is reframed as a threat to public peace or as divisiveness, and the substance of the disagreement never has to be argued. Christians should expect the translation and should answer as Paul did — not by denying what they hold, but by insisting the charge be stated accurately.

The mirror image of this sin belongs to the church itself, and it is worth naming. Ringleader in English carries the sense of a man who gathers a following to himself, and the New Testament has hard words for that within the congregation: men who draw away disciples after them, who cause divisions and offences contrary to the doctrine. Paul was protostates in the honest sense — first in the rank, first into the danger, and pointing away from himself: we preach not ourselves, but Christ Jesus the Lord. A leader who gathers a party around his own name has earned the English word in the sense Webster gives it, and no persecution is needed to make the charge stick.
roots_summary: Greek protostates (G4414), one standing first in rank; stasis (G4714), sedition or insurrection; hairesis (G139), a sect or party; loimos (G3061), a plague or pest.
roots_lines: Greek protostates (G4414) — the front-rank man; rendered ringleader, its only occurrence.
Greek stasis (G4714) — a standing up, an insurrection; rendered sedition, the charge Rome would hear.
Greek hairesis (G139) — a chosen party, a sect; rendered sect here and heresy at verse 14.
Greek loimos (G3061) — a plague, a pestilence; applied to a man as a pestilent fellow.
Greek Nazoraios (G3480) — a Nazarene; used here as a term of contempt for the church.
usage: “a ringleader of the sect of the Nazarenes” — the front-rank man, said as an accusation.
“a mover of sedition” — the charge framed for a Roman ear.
“after the way which they call heresy, so worship I” — Paul's answer.

etymology: Hebrew taar, a sheath, from a root meaning to lay bare — the case from which a blade is drawn. The English is Anglo-French escaubers, a sword-sheath. The word occurs once in Scripture, in a prophet's plea to a sword.
biblical_def: O thou sword of the LORD, how long will it be ere thou be quiet? put up thyself into thy scabbard, rest, and be still. Jeremiah is watching judgment fall on Philistia and cries out to the instrument itself to stop. The prayer is entirely understandable and it is refused. The next verse gives the answer, and it is the reason the passage matters: how can it be quiet, seeing the LORD hath given it a charge against Ashkelon, and against the sea shore? he hath appointed it. The sword cannot sheathe itself, because it is not acting on its own; it has been given a charge and an appointment. Three things stand together here and Scripture never separates them. God's judgments are real and terrible, and the prophet does not pretend otherwise. The prophet's grief at them is genuine and is recorded without rebuke — Jeremiah is not scolded for asking. And the judgment is nonetheless God's own, ordered and timed, and it will not stop before its appointment is fulfilled. A sword in a scabbard is a sword under restraint; the whole force of the image is that the restraint is God's to give and not the sword's to take. The same instrument appears in the New Testament transfigured: the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): the sheath of a sword; a case in which the blade of a sword is kept.
webster_full: SCABBARD, n. The sheath of a sword.
SHEATH, n. A case for the reception of a sword or other long and slender instrument.
SWORD, n. An offensive weapon worn at the side, used either for thrusting or cutting; emblem of vengeance, war, justice and authority.
APPOINT, v.t. To fix; to settle; to determine; to ordain by decree or decision.
CHARGE, n. That which is enjoined, committed, entrusted or delivered to another, implying care, custody or duty.
scriptures: Jeremiah 47:6
O thou sword of the LORD, how long will it be ere thou be quiet? put up thyself into thy scabbard, rest, and be still.
Jeremiah 47:7
How can it be quiet, seeing the LORD hath given it a charge against Ashkelon, and against the sea shore? there hath he appointed it.
Deuteronomy 32:35
To me belongeth vengeance, and recompence; their foot shall slide in due time: for the day of their calamity is at hand, and the things that shall come upon them make haste.
Ephesians 6:17
And take the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God:
corruption_summary: Divine judgment is widely treated as sub-Christian and edited out of the picture of God; Jeremiah shows a prophet who grieves the judgment, pleads against it, and still confesses that God appointed it.
corruption_paragraphs: The standard modern handling of passages like Jeremiah 47 is to treat them as an earlier and cruder stage of religion, superseded by the God revealed in Christ. That division cannot be maintained from the text. The New Testament quotes to me belongeth vengeance twice and applies it to the church's own day; the Lord spoke more about final judgment than any prophet before him; and the last book of the canon is full of a wrath poured out. A God who does not judge is not more loving but less just, and the cross itself is unintelligible without the wrath it turned away.

The opposite hardness is a piety that can recite the doctrine of judgment without grief. Jeremiah could not. He cries how long, he asks the sword to rest, and the Holy Spirit records the plea without a word of reproof — the same prophet who wrote Lamentations over his own people's ruin. Sound doctrine here is not the suppression of the cry but the holding of both: the judgment is God's and right, and the believer who watches it may weep. Abraham pleaded for Sodom; the Lord wept over Jerusalem before he pronounced its desolation.
roots_summary: Hebrew taar (H8593), a sheath or scabbard; chereb (H2719), a sword; shaqat (H8252), to be quiet; yaad (H3259), to appoint.
roots_lines: Hebrew taar (H8593) — a sheath; rendered scabbard, its only such rendering.
Hebrew chereb (H2719) — a sword; here called the sword of the LORD.
Hebrew shaqat (H8252) — to be quiet, to rest; what the prophet asks and is denied.
Hebrew yaad (H3259) — to appoint, to assign a time and place; there hath he appointed it.
Greek machaira (G3162) — a sword; the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God.
usage: “put up thyself into thy scabbard” — the prophet's plea to the sword.
“how can it be quiet” — the answer he receives.
“there hath he appointed it” — the judgment ordered and timed.

pos: n. pl. (words said over and over; babbling)
etymology: Greek battologeo, to stammer or babble, said to be formed in imitation of stuttering speech — to repeat the same syllables without meaning. The Authorized Version's vain repetitions renders the single verb.
biblical_def: But when ye pray, use not vain repetitions, as the heathen do: for they think that they shall be heard for their much speaking. The Lord is correcting a specific theory of prayer, and he states the theory plainly so that it can be rejected: the notion that God is moved by volume. The Greek battologeo imitates stammering — syllables repeated without meaning, on the assumption that the accumulation does the work. The prophets of Baal on Carmel are the biblical picture of it, crying from morning until noon. What the Lord gives as the reason against it is not that repetition is inherently wrong but that it misunderstands who is being addressed: be not ye therefore like unto them: for your Father knoweth what things ye have need of, before ye ask him. The Father already knows. Prayer therefore is not information supplied to God nor pressure applied to him; it is a child speaking to a Father who is already disposed to give. And having cleared the ground, the Lord immediately supplies the pattern, which is notable for its brevity and order: After this manner therefore pray ye: Our Father which art in heaven, Hallowed be thy name. It is worth observing that he does not forbid persistence. He commands it elsewhere, in the parables of the friend at midnight and the importunate widow. What he forbids is the mechanical repetition that treats words as currency.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): the act of repeating; a doing or saying again; recital; the act of rehearsing a second time.
webster_full: REPETITION, n. The act of repeating; a doing or saying again; iteration.
REPETITION, n. Recital from memory; rehearsal.
VAIN, a. Empty; worthless; having no substance, value or importance; fruitless; ineffectual.
PRAYER, n. In worship, a solemn address to the Supreme Being, consisting of adoration, confession, supplication and thanksgiving.
BABBLE, v.i. To utter words imperfectly or indistinctly; to talk idly or irrationally.
scriptures: Matthew 6:7
But when ye pray, use not vain repetitions, as the heathen do: for they think that they shall be heard for their much speaking.
Matthew 6:8
Be not ye therefore like unto them: for your Father knoweth what things ye have need of, before ye ask him.
Matthew 6:9
After this manner therefore pray ye: Our Father which art in heaven, Hallowed be thy name.
Hebrews 10:31
It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God.
corruption_summary: The verse is used to condemn all set forms of prayer, and ignored where prayer is in fact treated as a technique; the Lord forbids the theory that God is moved by quantity.
corruption_paragraphs: Some traditions have used Matthew 6:7 to rule out any written or repeated prayer, which proves more than the text will bear and more than the Lord intended — since in the very next breath he gives his disciples a form of words to use, and since the Psalter, the church's prayer book, contains a psalm with a refrain repeated twenty-six times. What is condemned is battologia: syllables piled up in the belief that the pile is what persuades. A rightly ordered liturgy is not that, and neither is the Lord's Prayer said with understanding. The rosary and its equivalents, where a fixed count is held to carry weight, are.

The extempore tradition is not exempt, and its version is harder to see because it produces no beads. Prayer becomes technique wherever the believer trusts something other than the Father's knowledge and goodness to secure the answer — the right formula, sufficient emotional intensity, the word-of-faith insistence that a request must be claimed in the correct terms, or simply length as a proof of earnestness. Every one of these is the heathen theory in Christian clothing. The Lord's remedy is doctrinal rather than technical: your Father knoweth what things ye have need of, before ye ask him.
roots_summary: Greek battologeo (G945), to babble or repeat idly; polulogia (G4180), much speaking; proseuchomai (G4336), to pray; ethnikos (G1482), heathen.
roots_lines: Greek battologeo (G945) — to stammer, to babble; rendered use vain repetitions, its only occurrence.
Greek polulogia (G4180) — much speaking, wordiness; rendered much speaking, its only occurrence.
Greek ethnikos (G1482) — heathen, of the nations; whose practice is named as the pattern to avoid.
Greek proseuchomai (G4336) — to pray; the ordinary New Testament verb.
Greek hagiazo (G37) — to hallow, to set apart as holy; the first petition of the pattern given.
usage: “use not vain repetitions” — the theory that volume persuades.
“your Father knoweth… before ye ask him” — the reason given.
“After this manner therefore pray ye” — the pattern supplied immediately.

pos: v. (to load too heavily; to burden beyond measure)
etymology: Greek epibareo, to be a weight upon, from epi, upon, and baros, a burden. The English compounds over with charge in its older sense of a load — the same sense that survives in the charge of a cannon or a beast of burden.
biblical_def: But if any have caused grief, he hath not grieved me, but in part: that I may not overcharge you all. Paul is writing about a man who had been disciplined by the Corinthian church, and the restraint in the sentence is remarkable. He declines to make the offence about himself — he hath not grieved me, but in part — and he checks his own language deliberately, that I may not overcharge you all, that is, that he may not lay a heavier weight on the congregation than the case requires. The word means to load beyond what a thing can bear. What follows is the fullest statement in the New Testament of the purpose of church discipline. Sufficient to such a man is this punishment, which was inflicted of many. The discipline had worked; it is therefore to stop. And the apostolic instruction is the reverse of what a congregation that has finally acted usually wants to hear: so that contrariwise ye ought rather to forgive him, and comfort him, lest perhaps such a one should be swallowed up with overmuch sorrow. The same root appears in the Lord's warning about hearts overcharged with surfeiting and drunkenness and the cares of this life. In both places the danger is a weight that a man was never built to carry, and in both the remedy is to put it down.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): to charge or load too heavily; to burden; to oppress; to fill to excess.
webster_full: OVERCHARGE, v.t. To charge or load to excess; to cloy; to oppress.
OVERCHARGE, v.t. To burden; to lay too heavy a load or burden on.
OVERCHARGE, v.t. To fill too full; to crowd too much.
BURDEN, n. That which is borne or carried; a load; that which is grievous, wearisome or oppressive.
SURFEITING, n. The act of feeding to excess; fullness and oppression of the system, occasioned by excessive eating and drinking.
scriptures: 2 Corinthians 2:5
But if any have caused grief, he hath not grieved me, but in part: that I may not overcharge you all.
2 Corinthians 2:6
Sufficient to such a man is this punishment, which was inflicted of many.
2 Corinthians 2:7
So that contrariwise ye ought rather to forgive him, and comfort him, lest perhaps such a one should be swallowed up with overmuch sorrow.
Luke 21:34
And take heed to yourselves, lest at any time your hearts be overcharged with surfeiting, and drunkenness, and cares of this life, and so that day come upon you unawares.
corruption_summary: Church discipline is either abandoned altogether or practised without its appointed end; Paul's instruction is that when the discipline has done its work the congregation must forgive, comfort, and stop.
corruption_paragraphs: Most congregations err by disuse. Discipline is felt to be unloving, membership means nothing in particular, and the New Testament's repeated instructions on the subject go unread. The cost falls on the erring member first, who is left undisturbed in a course Scripture says leads to death, and on the congregation second, which loses any meaningful witness about what it is to be a Christian. The Lord gave the procedure in Matthew 18 and Paul applied it in Corinth, and neither treats it as optional or as cruelty.

The opposite failure is the one this passage actually addresses, and it is the more grievous for being rarer only in appearance. A church that has finally brought itself to act often cannot bring itself to stop. The offender repents and the coldness remains; the discipline continues informally long after it has ended formally. Paul calls this overcharging — laying on a weight beyond what the case warrants — and warns of the specific outcome: lest perhaps such a one should be swallowed up with overmuch sorrow. The restoration is not a concession granted reluctantly. It is commanded, in the same voice and with the same authority as the discipline was.
roots_summary: Greek epibareo (G1912), to be a burden upon; baros (G922), a weight; epitimia (G2009), punishment or censure; katapino (G2666), to swallow up.
roots_lines: Greek epibareo (G1912) — to lay a weight upon; rendered overcharge, and be chargeable elsewhere.
Greek baros (G922) — a burden, a weight; the root of the loading image.
Greek epitimia (G2009) — a penalty, a censure; rendered punishment, its only occurrence.
Greek katapino (G2666) — to drink down, to swallow up; the danger to the over-disciplined man.
Greek bareo (G916) — to weigh down; rendered overcharged of the heart at Luke 21:34.
usage: “that I may not overcharge you all” — apostolic restraint in language.
“ye ought rather to forgive him, and comfort him” — the end of discipline.
“lest your hearts be overcharged” — the same word, of a loaded heart.

pos: v. (burned on the surface; cauterised into insensibility)
etymology: Greek kauteriazo, to brand or cauterise with a hot iron — the root of the English cauterise. A seared surface is one burned until the nerve is dead and it can no longer feel.
biblical_def: Speaking lies in hypocrisy; having their conscience seared with a hot iron. Paul is describing teachers who will arise in the latter times, and the metaphor is medical and horrifying. To cauterise is to burn tissue until the nerve dies; a seared conscience is one that has been burned past feeling. The point is not that these men have no conscience but that theirs no longer reports. They can speak lies without discomfort, which is what makes them effective and what makes the warning necessary. Paul traces the pedigree of their doctrine without euphemism: the Spirit speaketh expressly, that in the latter times some shall depart from the faith, giving heed to seducing spirits, and doctrines of devils. And he names the content, which is startling for how pious it sounds — forbidding to marry, and commanding to abstain from meats, which God hath created to be received with thanksgiving. The doctrine of devils in this passage is not licentiousness but a false austerity, a religion of prohibitions God never issued. Paul's verdict on such a system is given to Titus in one line: unto the pure all things are pure: but unto them that are defiled and unbelieving is nothing pure; but even their mind and conscience is defiled. A conscience is a faculty that can be trained, hardened, or destroyed, and Scripture treats its condition as a matter of life and death.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): burnt on the surface; cauterized; hardened; made insensible.
webster_full: SEAR, v.t. To burn on the surface; to scorch; to cauterize.
SEAR, v.t. To make callous or insensible; as, to sear the conscience.
SEARED, pp. Burnt on the surface; cauterized; hardened.
CAUTERIZE, v.t. To burn or sear with fire or a hot iron, as morbid flesh.
CONSCIENCE, n. The faculty, power or principle within us, which decides on the lawfulness or unlawfulness of our own actions and affections.
scriptures: 1 Timothy 4:2
Speaking lies in hypocrisy; having their conscience seared with a hot iron;
1 Timothy 4:1
Now the Spirit speaketh expressly, that in the latter times some shall depart from the faith, giving heed to seducing spirits, and doctrines of devils;
1 Timothy 4:3
Forbidding to marry, and commanding to abstain from meats, which God hath created to be received with thanksgiving of them which believe and know the truth.
Titus 1:15
Unto the pure all things are pure: but unto them that are defiled and unbelieving is nothing pure; but even their mind and conscience is defiled.
corruption_summary: Conscience is now treated as the final authority on right and wrong, when Scripture says it can be seared, defiled, or weak; and the doctrine of devils Paul names turns out to be an added austerity, not a licence.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern conscience has been promoted to the highest court: a man must be true to himself, and what he sincerely feels to be right is right for him. Scripture regards conscience as a real and important faculty and also as a fallible one. It can be weak and need instruction, defiled and need cleansing, or seared and past feeling altogether. Only Scripture binds absolutely. A conscience must be informed by the word of God before it can be safely obeyed, which is why the Reformers, who defended conscience against Rome so fiercely, always defended it as conscience captive to the word of God and never as conscience simply.

The second thing worth naming is what Paul identifies as the doctrine of devils. A reader expects debauchery. What he gets is forbidding to marry and commanding to abstain from meats — prohibitions stricter than God's own, imposed as marks of holiness. Rome made both of these law for its clergy and its calendar, and every movement that adds rules to Scripture as a measure of spirituality repeats the pattern. Added austerity looks like the opposite of a seared conscience and comes from the same root, because both replace the word of God as the rule: one by ignoring it, the other by improving on it.
roots_summary: Greek kauteriazo (G2743), to cauterise or brand; suneidesis (G4893), conscience; planos (G4108), seducing or deceiving; daimonion (G1140), a devil.
roots_lines: Greek kauteriazo (G2743) — to burn with a hot iron; rendered seared, its only occurrence.
Greek suneidesis (G4893) — conscience, co-knowledge; a faculty that can be weak, defiled, or destroyed.
Greek planos (G4108) — wandering, deceiving; rendered seducing spirits.
Greek daimonion (G1140) — a demon; whose doctrines turn out to be added prohibitions.
Greek hupokrisis (G5272) — play-acting, hypocrisy; the manner in which the lies are spoken.

“doctrines of devils” — identified as forbidding and abstaining.
“unto the pure all things are pure” — the answer to a false austerity.

pos: v. (to avoid; to turn away from; to keep clear of)
etymology: Greek periistemi, to stand around and so, in the middle voice, to turn oneself away from, to shun. Old English scunian, to abhor or avoid. Paul uses the word twice of profane babblings and once, negatively, of his own preaching.
biblical_def: But shun profane and vain babblings: for they will increase unto more ungodliness. The command is to turn away, and Paul gives a reason drawn from the nature of the thing rather than from the believer's comfort. Profane babbling does not stay where it is; they will increase unto more ungodliness, and he presses the image further — their word will eat as doth a canker, that is, it spreads like gangrene through healthy tissue. He then does something the modern church finds difficult and names two men, Hymenaeus and Philetus, and states their specific error. That is the apostolic pattern: the doctrine identified, the teachers named, the congregation warned. It is worth setting alongside Paul's other use of the same verb, where he tells the Ephesian elders that he had not shunned to declare unto them all the counsel of God. The two uses together give the balance. There are things a Christian must turn away from and there are things a minister must not turn away from, and a man who has them the wrong way round will avoid the hard doctrine and entertain the empty dispute. Paul's positive counsel follows immediately and is not withdrawal but pursuit: flee also youthful lusts: but follow righteousness, faith, charity, peace, with them that call on the Lord out of a pure heart.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): to avoid; to keep clear of; to refuse to meet; to escape; to eschew.
webster_full: SHUN, v.t. To avoid; to keep clear of; to refuse to meet or associate with.
SHUN, v.t. To decline; to neglect; as, to shun a duty.
ESCHEW, v.t. To flee from; to shun; to avoid, as something injurious.
PROFANE, a. Irreverent to any thing sacred; applied to persons; not sacred; secular; common.
CANKER, n. A disease incident to trees; a gangrene; anything that corrodes, corrupts or destroys.
scriptures: 2 Timothy 2:16
But shun profane and vain babblings: for they will increase unto more ungodliness.
2 Timothy 2:17
And their word will eat as doth a canker: of whom is Hymenaeus and Philetus;
2 Timothy 2:22
Flee also youthful lusts: but follow righteousness, faith, charity, peace, with them that call on the Lord out of a pure heart.
2 Timothy 3:5
Having a form of godliness, but denying the power thereof: from such turn away.
corruption_summary: Naming error and its teachers is treated as uncharitable, while the duty of avoidance is either abandoned entirely or expanded into a separatism that shuns brethren over trifles.
corruption_paragraphs: The instinct of the age is that a doctrine may be disputed but a teacher may not be named, and any Christian who names one is thought to have failed in love. Paul names Hymenaeus and Philetus in the sentence after he commands shunning, and elsewhere names Alexander, Demas, and Diotrephes. The reason is pastoral rather than combative: a congregation cannot avoid what it cannot identify. Naming an error while concealing its source leaves people defenceless in exactly the way the warning was meant to prevent, and Paul's image of a canker explains the urgency — gangrene is not contained by tact.

The opposite error turns a command about profane babbling into a programme of separation from brethren, so that secondary and tertiary differences become grounds for shunning and fellowship narrows to those who agree in everything. Paul's own balance is the corrective, and it sits three verses away: the servant of the Lord must not strive; but be gentle unto all men, apt to teach, patient, in meekness instructing those that oppose themselves. The same apostle who says shun says be gentle unto all men, and he says both to the same young minister in the same letter. The thing to be shunned is empty and profane talk that grows into ungodliness, not every brother who differs.
roots_summary: Greek periistemi (G4026), to turn oneself away from; kenophonia (G2757), empty sounding, vain babbling; gaggraina (G1044), a canker or gangrene; bebelos (G952), profane.

Greek kenophonia (G2757) — empty utterance; rendered vain babblings.
Greek bebelos (G952) — profane, unhallowed, open to all; rendered profane.
Greek gaggraina (G1044) — gangrene; rendered canker, its only occurrence.
Greek prokopto (G4298) — to advance, to increase; what the babblings do if not shunned.
usage: “shun profane and vain babblings” — turn away, because they spread.
“their word will eat as doth a canker” — the reason for urgency.
“I have not shunned to declare… all the counsel of God” — the same verb, the other duty.

etymology: Hebrew rosh, a bitter and poisonous herb, and so poison generally; the Authorized Version pairs it with poison in one verse. Latin venenum, a drug or poison, through Old French venim.
biblical_def: Their wine is the poison of dragons, and the cruel venom of asps. The line comes from the Song of Moses, and the figure is deliberate. Israel's enemies are described by what their vine produces, and what it produces is not wine but venom. The preceding verse sets it up — their vine is of the vine of Sodom, and of the fields of Gomorrah. Moses is saying that a corrupt root yields a poisonous fruit, and that the poison is in the thing itself rather than in its misuse. Paul reaches for the same image when he assembles his indictment of the whole human race from the Psalms: their throat is an open sepulchre; with their tongues they have used deceit; the poison of asps is under their lips. There the venom is located in speech, which is where James also locates it, calling the tongue an unruly evil, full of deadly poison. The consistent biblical use is worth noting. Venom in Scripture is not chiefly a figure for anger or cruelty in the abstract; it is most often a figure for what comes out of a man's mouth. That connects the image directly to the Lord's teaching that out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaketh, and that what defiles a man is what proceeds out of him. And the Song does not end in poison: to me belongeth vengeance, and recompence, says the LORD, and the judgment is his and not the injured party's.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): poison; matter fatal or injurious to life; spite; malice.
webster_full: VENOM, n. Poison; matter fatal or injurious to life; the poison of serpents.
VENOM, n. Spite; malice; as the venom of slander.
VENOMOUS, a. Poisonous; full of poison; noxious to animal life.
ASP, ASPIC, n. A small poisonous serpent of Egypt and Libya, whose bite occasions certain death.
POISON, n. Any substance which, when taken into the stomach or applied to the body, proves fatal or destructive to life.
scriptures: Deuteronomy 32:33
Their wine is the poison of dragons, and the cruel venom of asps.
Deuteronomy 32:35
To me belongeth vengeance, and recompence; their foot shall slide in due time: for the day of their calamity is at hand, and the things that shall come upon them make haste.
Romans 3:13
Their throat is an open sepulchre; with their tongues they have used deceit; the poison of asps is under their lips:
Ephesians 6:17
And take the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God:
corruption_summary: Destructive speech is minimised as personality or bluntness; Scripture calls it venom, traces it to the heart, and reserves the redress to God.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. No movement has laid claim to the word. The principle to recover is the seriousness Scripture attaches to the tongue. Paul places the poison of asps is under their lips inside his summary indictment of the whole race, alongside murder and the absence of the fear of God, and James says the tongue is set on fire of hell. A culture that prizes candour, and a church that excuses a sharp member as merely blunt, have both lost the category. The diagnosis Scripture gives is not a communication problem: out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaketh, and venom in the speech means venom at the root.

The second thing this passage settles is what the injured party may do. Moses places to me belongeth vengeance, and recompence two verses after the description of the poison, and Paul quotes the line twice in the New Testament, applying it directly to Christians who have been wronged — avenge not yourselves, but rather give place unto wrath. The redress is real, certain, and God's. That is what frees a believer from having to answer venom in kind, and it is why the only weapon named for the Christian's warfare is the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God.
roots_summary: Hebrew rosh (H7219), a bitter poison; chemah (H2534), heat, poison, fury; pethen (H6620), an asp; naqam (H5359), vengeance.
roots_lines: Hebrew rosh (H7219) — a poisonous herb, gall, venom; rendered poison in the same verse.
Hebrew chemah (H2534) — heat, and so venom or fury; rendered venom.
Hebrew pethen (H6620) — an asp, a venomous serpent; the creature named.
Hebrew naqam (H5359) — vengeance; claimed by the LORD as his own.
Greek ios (G2447) — poison, rust; the poison of asps at Romans 3:13 and the tongue's deadly poison in James.
usage: “the cruel venom of asps” — what a corrupt vine yields.
“the poison of asps is under their lips” — the venom located in speech.
“to me belongeth vengeance” — the redress reserved to God.

pos: v. (turned aside; missed the mark; deviated)
etymology: Greek astocheo, from a-, not, and stochos, a mark or aim — to miss the target, to fail of the aim. The English swerve is Old English sweorfan, to rub or turn aside.
biblical_def: From which some having swerved have turned aside unto vain jangling. Paul is describing men who wanted to be teachers of the law and had missed something first. The Greek astocheo is an archer's word — to miss the mark, to fail of the aim — and the question is what mark they missed. Paul has just named it: now the end of the commandment is charity out of a pure heart, and of a good conscience, and of faith unfeigned. The end is the target, the thing the commandment aims at, and it is love proceeding from three things — a clean heart, a conscience that works, and faith without pretence. Men who miss that target do not thereby stop teaching. They turn aside unto vain jangling — empty talk, disputation for its own sake — and Paul adds a devastating observation: desiring to be teachers of the law; understanding neither what they say, nor whereof they affirm. The confidence survives the comprehension. This is the permanent hazard of doctrinal seriousness, and the dictionary names it against itself as readily as against anyone: a man may hold sound positions, defend them vigorously, and have swerved from the mark those positions exist to serve. Paul does not answer error with less doctrine but with doctrine aimed where it belongs.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): to wander from any line prescribed, or from a rule of duty; to deviate; to depart.
webster_full: SWERVE, v.i. To wander; to rove; to stray; to deviate.
SWERVE, v.i. To wander from any line prescribed, or from a rule of duty; to depart; to deviate.
SWERVED, pp. Deviated; departed from the line or rule.
JANGLE, v.i. To quarrel in words; to altercate; to bicker; to wrangle.
AIM, n. The pointing or direction of a missile weapon; the direction of any thing to a particular point or object; intention; purpose.
scriptures: 1 Timothy 1:6
From which some having swerved have turned aside unto vain jangling;
1 Timothy 1:5
Now the end of the commandment is charity out of a pure heart, and of a good conscience, and of faith unfeigned:
1 Timothy 1:7
Desiring to be teachers of the law; understanding neither what they say, nor whereof they affirm.
2 Timothy 2:22
Flee also youthful lusts: but follow righteousness, faith, charity, peace, with them that call on the Lord out of a pure heart.
corruption_summary: Doctrine and love are regularly set against each other, one party abandoning precision for warmth and the other treating contention as a proof of soundness; Paul makes love the mark that doctrine aims at.
corruption_paragraphs: One party reads 1 Timothy 1:5 as a demotion of doctrine: since the end of the commandment is charity, precision must matter less than kindness, and controversy is itself the failure. That inverts Paul's argument. He is writing to charge Timothy that certain men teach no other doctrine, and the whole letter is an exercise in doctrinal precision. An archer who cares nothing for his aim does not hit the target by good will. Love is the mark, and sound doctrine is how the shot is aimed; a church that abandons the aim in the name of the target will hit neither.

The opposite party swerves in the direction this verse actually describes, and it is the temptation of the confessionally serious. A man may be exactly right about the ordo salutis and have a conscience he no longer consults and a faith that has become a position he defends. Paul's diagnosis of the swerved is not that they became liberal but that they turned to vain jangling — endless, heated, empty dispute — while still desiring the teacher's chair. The test he supplies is not softness but the three things named in verse 5: a pure heart, a good conscience, and faith unfeigned. Doctrine that produces none of these has missed what it was aimed at.
roots_summary: Greek astocheo (G795), to miss the mark; stochos, a target; mataiologia (G3150), vain talking; anupokritos (G505), unfeigned; agape (G26), charity.
roots_lines: Greek astocheo (G795) — to miss the aim; rendered swerved here and erred twice elsewhere in the Pastorals.
Greek mataiologia (G3150) — empty talking; rendered vain jangling, its only occurrence.
Greek telos (G5056) — the end, the goal aimed at; rendered the end of the commandment.
Greek agape (G26) — love; rendered charity, the mark the commandment aims at.
Greek anupokritos (G505) — without play-acting; rendered faith unfeigned.
usage: “some having swerved” — an archer's word, of missing the mark.
“the end of the commandment is charity” — the mark itself.
“understanding neither what they say” — confidence outliving comprehension.

pos: adv. (by deliberate choice; of set purpose)
etymology: Greek hekousios, willingly, voluntarily, of one's own accord — the opposite of what is done under compulsion or in ignorance. The English compounds will with -ful: full of one's own will.
biblical_def: For if we sin wilfully after that we have received the knowledge of the truth, there remaineth no more sacrifice for sins. The warning is among the most solemn in Scripture and it must be read for exactly what it says. Hekousios means voluntarily, of set purpose — and the old covenant background matters, since the law made provision by sacrifice for sins of ignorance and made none for the sin of a high hand. The writer is not describing a believer who falls, repents, and is restored; David murdered and was forgiven, Peter denied and was restored. He is describing deliberate, settled, high-handed apostasy by a man who had received the knowledge of the truth and trampled it. The description he gives leaves no room for a lesser reading: he hath trodden under foot the Son of God, and hath counted the blood of the covenant, wherewith he was sanctified, an unholy thing, and hath done despite unto the Spirit of grace. The reason no sacrifice remains is not that God's mercy has run short but that there is no other sacrifice; a man who has finally repudiated the one offering has nowhere left to go. What follows is meant to be felt: a certain fearful looking for of judgment and fiery indignation; and, it is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God. The writer's own conclusion about his readers is nevertheless confident: we are not of them who draw back unto perdition; but of them that believe to the saving of the soul.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): by design; with set purpose; obstinately; stubbornly.
webster_full: WILFULLY, adv. By design; with set purpose or intention.
WILFUL, a. Governed by the will without yielding to reason; obstinate; stubborn; perverse.
WILFUL, a. Intentional; premeditated; as wilful murder.
PRESUMPTUOUS, a. Bold and confident to excess; done with bold design or with contempt of divine law.
APOSTASY, n. An abandonment of what one has professed; a total desertion or departure from one's faith or religion.
scriptures: Hebrews 10:26
For if we sin wilfully after that we have received the knowledge of the truth, there remaineth no more sacrifice for sins,
Hebrews 10:27
But a certain fearful looking for of judgment and fiery indignation, which shall devour the adversaries.
Hebrews 10:29

Of how much sorer punishment, suppose ye, shall he be thought worthy, who hath trodden under foot the Son of God, and hath counted the blood of the covenant, wherewith he was sanctified, an unholy thing, and hath done despite unto the Spirit of grace?
Hebrews 10:31
It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God.
corruption_summary: The passage is used either to torment believers who have sinned seriously or to prove that a true Christian may finally perish; it describes high-handed apostasy and is given as a warning God uses to keep his own.
corruption_paragraphs: The pastoral damage done by misreading Hebrews 10:26 is considerable. Believers who have fallen badly conclude that they have committed the sin for which no sacrifice remains, and despair. The text does not describe them. It describes a man who has trodden the Son of God under foot, counted the blood of the covenant an unholy thing, and insulted the Spirit of grace — a settled and contemptuous repudiation, not a fall. The surest evidence that a person has not done this is that he fears he has; the man in view here is precisely the man who has stopped caring. A conscience still alive to the offence is the Spirit's work, not the absence of it.

Doctrinally the passage is pressed to overturn the perseverance of the saints. The Reformed answer does not soften the warning; it reads it alongside the same book's assurance and the Lord's own words that his sheep shall never perish, neither shall any man pluck them out of his hand. Those who finally fall away were never truly his — they went out from us, but they were not of us. And the warning is not thereby made idle. God preserves his people through means, and this passage is one of them: a real danger, solemnly stated, which the Spirit uses to keep believers from the road that leads there. The writer applies it that way himself, and then tells his readers he is persuaded of better things concerning them.

Greek epignosis (G1922) — full or precise knowledge; what the apostate had received.
Greek katapateo (G2662) — to trample underfoot; rendered trodden under foot the Son of God.

“counted the blood of the covenant… an unholy thing” — the man described.
“we are not of them who draw back” — the writer's conclusion about his readers.

pos: n. (one who speaks on behalf of another)
etymology: Hebrew dabar, to speak, in a construction meaning he shall speak for thee. The English compound is plain: the man who speaks. The word occurs once, of Aaron appointed to speak for Moses.
biblical_def: And he shall be thy spokesman unto the people: and he shall be, even he shall be to thee instead of a mouth, and thou shalt be to him instead of God. The arrangement is made after Moses has exhausted his objections at the burning bush, and the narrative does not present it as a triumph. The anger of the LORD was kindled against Moses, and then Aaron was given. God had already answered the objection directly — who hath made man's mouth? and, I will be with thy mouth, and teach thee what thou shalt say — and Moses had asked again to be excused. The concession granted is real and is not a rebuke only; Aaron genuinely serves, and God uses him. But the structure deserves attention because it establishes a pattern that runs through Scripture. Moses receives the word and Aaron speaks it: thou shalt speak unto him, and put words in his mouth. God restates the relation in the same terms later — see, I have made thee a god to Pharaoh: and Aaron thy brother shall be thy prophet. A spokesman in the biblical sense has no message of his own. His entire authority is the message he was given, which is exactly the standing of every prophet, and of every preacher since. The office is high and the man in it is a mouth.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): one who speaks for another; one deputed to speak in the name of another.
webster_full: SPOKESMAN, n. One who speaks for another.
SPOKESMAN, n. One who is deputed to speak in the name or behalf of another person or of a body of men.
MOUTH, n. The aperture in the head of an animal by which it utters sounds; the instrument of speech.
PROPHET, n. One that foretells future events; one who speaks by divine inspiration, or by the impulse of the Holy Spirit.
DEPUTE, v.t. To appoint and send with a special commission to act in the place of another.
scriptures: Exodus 4:16
And he shall be thy spokesman unto the people: and he shall be, even he shall be to thee instead of a mouth, and thou shalt be to him instead of God.
Exodus 4:14

And the anger of the LORD was kindled against Moses, and he said, Is not Aaron the Levite thy brother? I know that he can speak well. And also, behold, he cometh forth to meet thee: and when he seeth thee, he will be glad in his heart.
Exodus 4:15
And thou shalt speak unto him, and put words in his mouth: and I will be with thy mouth, and with his mouth, and will teach you what ye shall do.
Exodus 7:1
And the LORD said unto Moses, See, I have made thee a god to Pharaoh: and Aaron thy brother shall be thy prophet.
corruption_summary: Preaching is widely treated as the speaker's own contribution, with Scripture supplying material; the biblical spokesman has no message of his own and is answerable for delivering another's.
corruption_paragraphs: Where the sermon is built around the preacher's insight, experience, or personality, with texts recruited to support it, the office has been inverted. Aaron's commission is the model and it is severe in its simplicity: Moses puts words in his mouth, and he speaks them. Every prophet after him says the same thing in the same way — thus saith the LORD — and Paul describes the ministry as stewardship, where the one thing required in stewards is that a man be found faithful. A spokesman who improves on his message has not enriched it; he has stopped being a spokesman.

Aaron's later history supplies the warning that belongs with the office, and Scripture does not spare him. The man appointed to speak for Moses is the same man who, left alone at the foot of the mountain, made the golden calf and then explained it with one of the least convincing sentences in the canon: there came out this calf. Eloquence was his qualification and it did not preserve him. The gift of speech is a real gift and is no protection whatever against the fear of the people, which is what actually moved him. A church choosing men to speak for God should weigh Exodus 32 alongside Exodus 4.
